title: Special (child-resistant) packaging for oral prescription drugs under the Poison Prevention Packaging Act
subtopic: Poison prevention packaging of prescription drugs
rule_summary: The Poison Prevention Packaging Act of 1970 (15 U.S.C. 1471-1476) lets the Consumer Product Safety Commission establish special packaging standards for household substances, a term that includes a drug as defined in 21 U.S.C. 321 that is customarily produced or distributed for sale for consumption or use, or customarily stored, by individuals in or about the household. Package means the immediate container or wrapping in which the substance is contained for consumption, use or storage by individuals in or about the household, and does not include a shipping container or outer wrapping used by retailers to ship or deliver the substance to consumers unless it is the only such container or wrapping. Special packaging means packaging designed or constructed to be significantly difficult for children under five years of age to open or obtain a toxic or harmful amount of the substance within a reasonable time and not difficult for normal adults to use properly, but does not mean packaging which all such children cannot open or obtain a toxic or harmful amount within a reasonable time (15 U.S.C. 1471; 16 CFR 1700.1). Under 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10), any drug for human use that is in a dosage form intended for oral administration and that is required by Federal law to be dispensed only by or upon an oral or written prescription of a practitioner licensed by law to administer such drug shall be packaged in accordance with 16 CFR 1700.15(a), (b) and (c), except for the substances listed in 1700.14(a)(10)(i)-(xxiv), which include sublingual dosage forms of nitroglycerin; sublingual and chewable forms of isosorbide dinitrate in dosage strengths of 10 milligrams or less; cyclically administered oral contraceptives in manufacturers' mnemonic dispenser packages that rely solely upon the activity of one or more progestogen or estrogen substances; anhydrous cholestyramine in powder form; unit dose forms of potassium supplements containing not more than 50 milliequivalents of potassium per unit dose; methylprednisolone tablets in packages containing not more than 84 mg; prednisone tablets dispensed in packages containing no more than 105 mg; medroxyprogesterone acetate tablets; and hormone replacement therapy products that rely solely upon the activity of one or more progestogen or estrogen substances; each listed exemption carries its own stated form, strength or package limits. Under 16 CFR 1700.15(a) and (b), special packaging must continue to function with the effectiveness specifications when in contact with the substance and for the number of openings and closings customary for its size and contents, and must have, when tested under 16 CFR 1700.20, child-resistant effectiveness of not less than 85 percent without a demonstration and not less than 80 percent after a demonstration (not less than 80 percent for unit packaging) and, except for aerosol and metal-container products, senior adult use effectiveness of not less than 90 percent. Under 16 CFR 1700.15(c), special packaging for substances subject to that paragraph shall not be reused. Under 16 CFR 1700.14(c), special packaging standards for listed drugs are in addition to any packaging requirements of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or its regulations or of any official compendia recognized by that act. Under 15 U.S.C. 1476(a), while a Commission standard is in effect for a household substance, no State may establish or continue in effect a special packaging standard (or exemption or related requirement) for that substance which is not identical to the federal standard, subject to 1476(b), which lets a State establish a non-identical standard for a household substance for its own use if it provides a higher degree of protection, and 1476(c), under which the Commission may by regulation exempt a State standard on the State's application.
exam_relevance: Tests when an oral prescription drug must go out in child-resistant packaging, the statutory meaning of special packaging (resistant, not childproof), the listed exemptions that come up at the counter, the bar on reusing special packaging, and the preemption of non-identical State packaging standards.

exceptions: The drugs listed in 16 CFR 1700.14(a)(10)(i)-(xxiv), each within its stated form, strength or package limits.
Dispensing in noncomplying packages when directed in the prescriber's order or requested by the purchaser under 15 U.S.C. 1473(b).
common_confusions: Treating special packaging as childproof; the definition excludes a requirement that all children be unable to open it.
Assuming every nitroglycerin or oral contraceptive product is exempt; the exemptions are limited to the listed dosage forms and package types.
Reusing a special-packaging vial for a refill.
verification_notes: 15 U.S.C. 1471-1476 read on uscode.house.gov (chapter 39A, current edition) and 16 CFR 1700.1, 1700.14, 1700.15 and 1700.20 read in the current eCFR text during the authoring session of 2026-09-16 to 2026-09-17. Section 1475 is repealed.
